sentences.text: The 33 sermons on Nibbana were delivered by the Venerable Bhikkhu Katukurunde Jnanananda
in Sinhala at Mitrigala Nisarana Vinaya Forest Hermitage.
They were translated into English by the same Venerable monk,
presently residing at Potkulkala Forest Hermitage in Khandgidra, Devalagam.
This is peaceful, this is excellent, namely the stilling of all preparations, the relinquishment
of all assets, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction.
With the permission of the Most Venerable Great Preceptor and the Assembly of the Venerable
Meditative Mass, this is the sixteenth sermon in the series of sermons on Nibbana.
In the course of our discussion of the Bhaya Sutta in our last sermon, we drew attention
to the wide gap that exists between the sensory experience of the worldly and that experience
the Arant gets through the Eye of Wisdom.
It is the same gap that obtains between the two terms Papancha and Nipapancha.
In sensory experience which is based on worldly expressions, worldly usages and worldly concepts,
there is a discrimination between a thing to be grasped and the one who grasps or in other
words, a subject-object relationship.
There is always a bifurcation, a dichotomy, in the case of sensory perception.
If there is a scene, there has to be something seen and one who sees, that is the logic.
In the Bhaya Sutta, beginning with, in the scene there will be just a scene, the Buddha proclaimed
to the ascetic Bhaya, a brief exhortation on Dhamma, which enables one to transcend the
above narrow viewpoint and attain the state of non-proliferation or Nipapancha.
There is nothing to see, no one to see, only a scene is there.
The cause of all these conceptual proliferation of Papancha in the world is contact.
The arahans understood this by their insight into the fact that the seen, the heard, the
sensed and the cognized are simply so many collocations of conditions which come together
for a moment due to contact, only to break up and get dispersed the next moment.
What is called the seen, the heard, the sensed and the cognized are, for the world, in so
many things.
But to the wisdom eye of the arahans, they appear as mere conglomerations of conditions,
dependent on contact, which momentarily come together and then get dispersed.
This insight into the dependence on contact, Phasam Patitya, is the very essence of the law
of dependent arising, Patitya Samuppad, it is equivalent to seeing the law of dependent arising
itself.
In order to transcend the narrow point of view limited to the basis of sense contact or the
sixth sense fears and realize the state of Nibbana indicated by the words vinyanam, anidassanam,
anantam, sabbato, pabham, consciousness which is non-manifestative, endless, lustrous on all
sides, one has to see in the cessation of contact.
In a certain discourse in the Muttalindavagva of the Udana, the Buddha has declared in a
verse of uplift that the cessation of contact comes about only by doing away with that it
brings about contact.
The wandering ascetics of other sects grew jealous of the Buddha and his congregation
of monks because of their own loss of gain and honor and began to hurt abuse on monks
in the village and in the forest.
A group of monks came and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha's response to it was only a plan of job.
Udana actually means a spontaneous utterance of George and the verse he uttered was Satchavan,
but it embodied an instruction on Dhamma and the norm of Dhamma as well.

saga, relinquishment of all assets, and nirupadhi, the assetless, used with reference to Nippon.
In a number of previous sermons we happened to explain the concept of upadhi to some extent,
as and when the terms upadhi and patini saga came up. To refresh our memory, we may summarize
all that now. What is the concept of upadhi or assets recognized by the world? Whatever
that bolsters of the ego, be it gold, silver, pearls, gems, money, house and property, deposits
and assets. All these are reckoned as upadhi in general. But when considered from the point
of view of Dhamma, upadhi in a deeper sense stands for these fivefold grasping groups,
panchupadana khanda. Upadana khanda literally means groups of grasping. Groups of grasping
do not necessarily imply that there are material objects to be grasped. But the world ring overcome
by that triple proliferation of cravings, conceits and views, and carried away by the worldly
conventions, imagines those groups of grasping as things grasped and deposited. The concept
of upadhi as assets as a result of this tendency to think of groups of grasping as things grasped
and deposited. So it turns out to be a question of viewpoint. Craving, conceits and views prompt
one to look upon all what one has grasped so far and what one hopes to grasp in the future
as things one is grasping right now. One thinks of them as things deposited in a safe. The worldlings
are holding on to such a mass of assets. Nibbana is the relinquishment of all such assets accumulated
in the mind. In order to relinquish these assets, there must be some kind of understanding and
enlightenment. The vanity of all these assets has to be seen through the light of wisdom.
It is only by seeing their vanity that the assets are relinquished. In fact, it is not so much a deliberate
giving up of assets as a sequential liquidation. In a previous sermon, we gave an illustration of the situation
that precipitates relinquishment. Let us bring it up again. We found the cinema quite helpful as an illustration.
In explaining the phenomenon of relinquishment of assets with reference to the cinema, we described how the assets
accumulated in the minds of the audience, that is, the assets proper to the cinema world, woven around the story
that is filmed, are automatically abandoned when the cinema hall gets lit up. Then one understands the illusory nature
of what has been going on. It is that understanding, that enlightenment, which precipitates the giving up or relinquishment of assets.
To go a step further in this illustration, when light came on, the Sankharas or preparations pertaining to the film show
got exposed for what they are. In fact, Sankhara is a world that has associations with the dramatic tradition
in its relation to the acting of actors and actresses down to their makeup, which is so artificial and spurious.
When the cinema hall gets lit up all of a sudden, one who has been enjoying the film show is momentarily thrown out of the cinema world,
because those preparations are pacified or nullified . As a consequence of it, the heap of experiences which he had hitherto regarded as real and genuine
in the scene, lose their sanction. Those assets get liquidated or relinquished .
In their absence, that craving necessary for the appreciation or enjoyment of the scenes to come becomes extinct .

When craving is gone, the floridity of the scenes to come also fades away Viraga.
With that fading away or decoloration, the film show ceases for the person concerned,
Nirodha, though technically the movie is going on.
Because of the association, all the fires of defilements proper to the cinema world
with which he was burning, kept extinguished, Nibban.
So, here we have the full gamut of the cinema simile as an illustration for Nibban.
This kind of awakening in the cinema world gives us a clue to the fact that the assets, upadhi,
are relinquished through an understanding born of enlightenment in the light of wisdom.
This, in fact, is something that should be deeply ingrained into our minds.
Therefore, we shall endeavor to give some more illustrations to that defect.
In our everyday life, too, we sometimes see and hear of instances where assets get relinquished due to understanding.
Someone heaps up a huge bundle of currency notes of the highest denomination,
deposits it in his safe, and keeps watch and ward over it day and night.
One fine morning, he wakes up to hear that for some reason or other,
that currency note has been fully devalued by law the previous night.
How does he look upon the values of knots in his safe now?
For him, it is now a mere heap of papers.
The craving, conceit and view he had earlier in regard to the notes are completely gone.
The banknotes are no longer valid.
He might as well make a bonfire of it.
So, this is some sort of relinquishment of assets in the world, however temporary it may be.
Another person gets a sudden transfer and is getting ready to leave for his new station.
His immovable assets he is forced to leave behind, but his movable assets he hurriedly gathers up to take with him.
The vehicle has already come and is tooting impatiently, signalling delay.
It is well past time, but his preparations are not finished.
Time pressed in hot haste, he is running here and there.
At last, when he can delay no longer, he grabs the utmost he can take and darts to the doorstep.
Just then he wakes up.
It was only a dream.
The transfer came in a dream.
No real vehicle.
No real preparation.
Only a panting for nothing.
So, here we have an awakening peculiar to the dream world.
This is an instance of letting go of assets connected with the dream.
We go through such experiences quite often.
Of course, we take it for granted that when we pass from the dream world to the real world,
the assets proper to the dream world drop off.
But are we sure that in leaving the dream world, we are entering a real world?
Like, is awakening from a dream a true awakening when considered from the point of view of the dhamma?
Do we actually open our eyes when we awaken from a dream?
Terms like Buddha, Bodhi, Bodhi and Sambodhi convey the sense of awakening as well as understanding.
Sometimes in the dhamma, the emphasis is on the sense of awakening.
Here, then, is a kind of awakening.
Expressions like dhamma chakhu, dhamma eye, panya chakhu, wisdom eye, and chakhu mudapadi, the eye arose.
We speak of an arising of some sort of an eye.
We already have eyes.
All this goes to show that in the context of Nibbana, where we are concerned with the deep aspects of the dhamma,
the awakening from a dream is not a true awakening.
It is only a passage from one dream world to another.
But, let us see how the concept of Upadhi, or assets, goes deeper.
What lies before us is the dream of samsara.
In order to awaken from this dream, we have to understand, somehow,
the vanity of all assets connected with the dream, that is samsara.
The fact that this understanding also comes through some illumination,
we have already explained the other day in our discussion of the Pian of Joy at the end of the Baya Sutra.
As we pointed out, then, the world of the Sixth Sense basis,
with the warnings regarded as their world,
when examined against the background of that Udanaverse,
reveals itself to be no more than six narrow beams of light,
appearing through a solidly thick curtain, namely, the darkness of Dalisha.
We happened to mention the other day that the sun, the moon, and the stars shine precisely because of the presence of darkness.
In the non-manifestative consciousness, which is infinite and lustrous all around,
sun, moon, and stars are not manifest because there is absolutely no darkness for them to shine for.
Even the formless, which is the penumbra of form, disappears in their penetrative luster of system.
So, the relinquishment of all assets in Bana is not like the other temporary awakenings already mentioned.
Those three instances of awakening are of a temporary nature.
The awakening in the cinema world is extremely short-lived.
That film fan, although he became disenchanted with the scenes because of the unexpected sudden illumination of the cinema hall,
when it is dark again, influxes of sensuality, existence, and ignorance so overwhelm him that he gets engrossed in the cinema world as before.
The case of the devalued currency note is also like that.
Though the cravings, conceits, and waves about the devalued note are gone, one still runs after notes that are valid.
As for the awakening from a dream, we all know that it is temporary.
When again we go to sleep, we have dreams.
But the awakening in Nibban is not of such a temporary character.
Why?
Because all the influxes that lead one into the samsaric slumber with its dreams of recurrent births are made extinct in the light of that perfect knowledge of realization.
That is why the term Mazavakya, extinction of influxes, is used in the discourses as an epithet of Nibban.
The Arathas accomplish this feat in the concentration on the fruit of Arathut, Arathapala Samadhi.
Though there are enough instances of references to this Arathapala Samadhi in the discourses, they are very often interpreted differently.
As we have already seen in the context of that verse of uplift in the Bhaya Sutta,
some discourses alluding to the nature of a Narahant's mind have been misinterpreted so much so that there is a lot of confusion in regard to the concept of Nibban.
As a matter of fact, that concentration peculiar to a Narahant is of an extraordinary type.
It baffles the worldlings' powers of understanding.
This can well be inferred from the following verse of the Ratana Sutta.
That pure concentration which the supremely awakened one extolled, that concentration which the noble ones called immediate, there is no concentration comparable to it.
This is the excellent jewel nature of the Dhamma.
By the power of this truth, may there be well-being.
This incomparable and extraordinary concentration has given rise to many problems concerning the concept of Nibban.
The extraordinariness of this concentration of the Arathapala Samadhi is to some extent connected with the term Anantarika, referred to above.
Now let us turn our attention to the significance of this term.
The verse says that the concentration of the Arathapala is also known as Anantarika.
The term Anantarika is suggestive of an extraordinary aspect of the realization of Nibbana.
Immediately after the extinction of the requirements through the knowledge of the path of Arathapala, one realizes Nibbana, the cessation of existence or the cessation of the sixth sense basis.
As we mentioned earlier, it is as if the results are out as soon as one has written for an examination.
One need not wait for the results. Realization is immediate.
There is a special term to denote this experience of realization, namely Anya.
It is a highly significant term derived from Ajaanati, to know fully.
Anya is full comprehension.
The concentration of the fruit of Paranthut is also called Anya Phara Samadhi and Anya Vimokha.
Anya carries with it a high degree of importance.
We come across in the Sutra terminology a number of the
of terms derived from the root nya to know namely sanya, vinyana, panya, nyana, abhinya, parinya,
anya. Sanya is perception. Vinyana is radically discriminative knowledge. Panya is distinctive
knowledge. Nyana is knowledge as such. Abhinya is specialized knowledge. Parinya is comprehensive
knowledge. Anya is that final knowledge of certitude through realization. The high degree of importance
attached to anya is revealed by the following two verses in Dhiti Bhuttaka. Sekhassa sekha
manassa ujumagganu svarino. Khyasmin pathaman jnanan tato anya anantra. Tato anya vimuttas
nyana veho ditadino. Akuppa me vimuttiti bhavasanyo janakhe.
To the disciple in higher training, as he fares along, training according to the straight
path, there arises first the knowledge of extinction and then immediately the final knowledge of
certitude. And to that steadfast such like one, thus released by final knowledge of certitude,
there arises the thought, unshakable is my deliverance, upon the destruction of fetters
of existence. It is evident from these two verses that the realization referred to is
in many ways final and complete. In point of fact, these two verses have been presented
by the Buddha in this context by way of defining three things relevant to the realization of
Nibbara. These three are called faculties, Indriya. They are 1. Ananyatanyasamitindriya,
2. Anyindriya, 3. Anyatavindriya. The term Anya is implicit even in the faculty called
Ananyatanyasamitindriya. Ananyatanyasamitindriya means, I shall know what has not been fully
known. This is the definition of what in the verse is referred to as khayasmi pathmanyana.
First, there is the knowledge of extinction. The knowledge of the extinction of the defilements
is called Ananyatanyasamitindriya in this context. The words Tato Vanya Anantara and then immediately
the final knowledge of certitude refer to that faculty of final knowledge or Anyindriya.
The knowledge that prompts the conviction unshakable is my deliverance is the knowledge and vision
of deliverance, which is defined as Anyatavindriya. It refers to one who is endowed with the final
knowledge of certitude. The difference between Anyindriya and Anyatavindriya is a subtle one.
For instance, the expression Guptavi Pavarito, one has finished eating and made a sign of refusal,
decisively shows that one has had one's fill. Similarly, it is that Anyatavindriya note the past
active participle which prompts the words, unshakable is my deliverance, akuppame vimuddhi.
The knowledge and vision of deliverance is reassuring to that extent.
As the above quoted verse from the Ratanasutta makes it clear, this unique and extraordinary
concentration has been extolled by the Buddha in various discourses. But for some reason or other,
the commentators have simply glossed over references to it. Though they sometimes expatiate on a
particle of mere grammatical interest, it does not take up for comment a few such discourses.
In the section of the Elements in the Anguttara Nikaya, there comes a discourse called Sandhasutta.
The Buddha gives to Venerable Sandha a description of a level of concentration characteristic of an
excellent thoroughbred of a man. It is a strange type of concentration. One who has that concentration
is described as follows.
So, the meaning of the Nisarjhati, Napaang Nisarjhati, Napaang Nisarjhati, Napaang Nisarjhati,
Napaang Nisarjhati, Nakaasananan chatanang Nisarjhati, Nanyanan chatanang Nisarjhati,
Nanyan sanyanasanjhati, Naitalokang Nisarjhati, Naitalokang Nisarjhati, Naparlokang Nisarjhati,
Nampidang Dittang Sutang Mutang Ninyatang Patthang Pariyasidang Anujarjhati Manasa,
Tampi Nisarjhati, Najayayati, Najayati Cepanam.
In this discourse, the Buddha gives as an illustration the musing of a thoroughbred of a horse, which
we shall drop for brevity's sake. The musing of an excellent thoroughbred of a man is described
as follows. He muses not dependent on earth, water, fire, air, the sphere of infinite space,
the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither perception
nor non-perception. He muses not dependent on this world or on the world beyond whatever is seen,
heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, traversed by the mind, dependent on all that
he muses not. And yet he does muse.
Moreover, Sandha, to him that's musing, the Devasit Indra with Brahma and with Prajapati,
even from afar, bowed down, saying,
Homage to you, O thoroughbred of a man! Homage to you, O most excellent of men! What it is
on which you go on musing, we are at a loss to comprehend.
Though all possible objects of concentration are negated, the Buddha affirms that he does
must muse. Venerabha Sandha, out of curiosity, inquires, but then how Lord does that thoroughbred
of a man muse? The Buddha explains that while in that state of concentration, the perception
of earth in earth, for instance, is gone for him.
Patavya Patavisanya Vibhuta Hote. So also in the case of other objects of their senses,
such as water, fire, air, down to whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought
after, and traversed by the mind. The verb Vibhuta repeatedly used in this connection is
however differently interpreted in the commentary. It is paraphrased by Pākata, which means clearly
manifest. This interpretation seems to distort the meaning of the entire passage. It is true
that in certain contexts, Vibhuta and Avibhuta are taken to mean manifest and unmanifest, since
Vibhava is a word which seems to have undergone some semantic development. However, its primary
sense is sufficiently evident in the Sutta terminology. For instance, the twin term Bhava-Vibhava stands
for existence and non-existence. In this context too, Vibhuta seems to have a negative sense,
rather than the sense of being manifest. Hence our rendering. The perception of earth is gone
wrong for him. It is obvious enough by the recurrent negative particle in the first part of the
Sutta, neva-pata-vegnis-saya-jhayati, na-apangis-saya-jhayati, etc., that all those perceptions are
negated and not affirmed as manifest. The commentator seems to have missed the true import of the
Sutta when he interprets Vibhuta to mean manifest. If further proof is required, we may quote instances
where the word Vibhuta is used in the Suttas to convey such senses as gone, departed or
transcendent. In one of the verses we happened to quote earlier from the Kalahivada Sutta,
there was the question posed, Kisming Vibhuta in a Pusanti Pasa. When what is not there, do
touch us do not touch? The verse that follows gives the answer Rūpe Vibhuta na Pusanti Pasa.
When form is not there, touch us do not touch. In this context too, Vibhuta implies absence.
A clear instance comes in the Pusala Manu Puscha of the Parayanamagya in the Sutta Nipat, namely,
the term Vibhuta Rūpa Sanyis occurring in one of the verses there. The canonical commentary
Chuluniddes, which the commentator often draws upon, also paraphrases the term with the words
Vigata, Atikkanta, Samatikkanta, Viti Vakta, gone, transcendent, fully transcendent and superseded.
So the word Vibhuta in the passage in question definitely implies the absence of all those
perceptions in that concentration. This then is a unique concentration. It has none of the objects
which the worldlings usually associate with the level of concentration. We come across another
question.

Whereas the passage quartered earlier began with so neva pattering his side jhāyati,
he muses not dependent on earth, and ended with the emphatic assertion, jhāyati chappana,
and yet he does muse, here we have a restatement of it in terms of perception, beginning with
neva pataviyāṁ, patavisanyīya, and ending with sanyi chappanas.
The Buddha answers in the affirmative, and on being questioned as to how it is possible,
he gives the following explanation.
Here in Ānanda, a monk is dust conscious, Āvāṁ sanyi. This is peaceful, this is excellent,
namely the stealing of all preparation, the relinquishment of all, as it is possible.
The destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction. It is thus Ānanda that there could
be for a monk such an attainment of concentration.
This in fact is the theme of all our sermons. Venerable Ānanda of course rejoiced in the
Buddha's words, but approached Venerable Sāribhuta also and put forward the same question.
Venerable Sāribhuta gave the same answer verbatim. Then Venerable Ānanda gave expression
to a joyous approbation.
Ācariyaṁ āaso, abhutaṁ āaso, yatrahi nāma sattu ca sāvakasa ca attena attaṁ,
vyanjanīna vyanjanāṁ saṁ sandhissati, samissati, nabigahissati, yadidāṁ aggapadasmi.
Friend, it is wonderful, it is marvellous that there is perfect conformity between the statements
of the teacher and the disciple to the letter and to the spirit without any discord on the question
of the highest level of attainment. These last words in particular make it sufficiently
clear that this concentration is ārātaphala samādhi, the concentration proper to an ārhaṁ.
Here then is the experience of Nibbāna, extraordinary and unique. Quite a number of discourses touch
upon this samādhi. Let us take up some of the more important references. Venerable Ānanda is seen to pose the same question
rephrased on yet another occasion. It runs thus.
Siyāna nukoh bante tathālupo samādhi patilābho, yathā,
na cakkum manasikareya, na ropang manasikareya, na sotang manasikareya, na saddang manasikareya,

Could there be Lord for a monk such an attainment of concentration
wherein he will not be attending to the eye, nor to form, nor to the ear, nor to sound,
nor to the nose, nor to smell, nor to the tongue, nor to taste, nor to the body, nor to touch,
nor to earth, nor to water, nor to fire, nor to air, nor to the sphere of infinite space,
nor to the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor to the sphere of nothingness,
nor to the sphere of neither perception, nor to this world, nor to the world beyond,
whatever is seen, heard, sensed, colonized, attained, sought after, traversed by the mind,
even to that he will not be attending, and yet he will be attending.
There could be such a concentration, says the Buddha,
and when Rupala Ananda rejoins with his inquisitive, how Lord could there be?
Then the Buddha gives the following explanation, which tallies with the one earlier given.
Idhananda bhikkhu evang manasi karvati.
Etang santang etang panitang yadidang sabbasamkhara samato sabbhupadhi pati nisaggo
tannakhyo viragao nirodho nimbānat
evang kho Ananda siyabhikkhu no tatharupo samadhi patilabhu.
Here in Ananda, a monk attends thus,
This is peaceful, this is excellent,
namely the stilling of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets,
the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction.
It is thus, Ananda, that there could be such an attainment of concentration.

The general trend of this verse seems to imply something like this.
The worldlings usually believe that one has to have some form of perception or other.
But the one referred to in this verse is not percipient with any such perception.
As if to forestall the question, whether he is then in a swoon, there is the negation,
na visagya sanyi.
A possible alternative, like a plane of existence,
divide of perception, is also avoided by the emphatic assertion,
no piya sanyi.
Yet another possibility that he has gone beyond perception or resigned at it,
is rejected as well with the words,
The third line says that it is to one thus endowed that form ceases to exist,
while the last line seems to give an indication as to why it is so.
Sanyani dana hi papanchya sankha.
For reckonings born of proliferation have perception as their source.
The nature of these reckonings we have already discussed at length.
The conclusion here given is that they are rooted in papanchya.
Now the passages we have so far quoted are suggestive of such a state of consciousness.
Briefly stated, even the emphatic knot characteristic of these discourses is sufficient proof of it.
For instance, in the first discourse we took up for discussion,
there is the recurrent phrase,
But at the end of it all comes the emphatic assertion,
Chāyati-chapana.
Nemadilas he does muse.
Similarly, the passage dealing with the sanya aspect starts with neva pataviyam patavisanyi,
He is neither conscious, literally percipient, of earth in earth,
followed by a long list of negations,
only to end up with an emphatic sanyi-chapanas,
but nevertheless he is conscious.
So also in the passage which takes up the attending aspect
and winds up with the assertion,
Manasi-chapana kareja,
and yet he will be attending.

The arahata phalas
This is obvious enough even if we take into consideration the occurrence of the term Papancha
Sankha in the last line of the verse in question. The worldly concepts born of the prolific tendency
of the mind are rooted in perception. That is precisely why perception has to be transcended.
That is also the reason for our emphasis on the need for freedom from the sixth sense
basis and from contact. The abandonment of Papancha Sankha is accomplished at this
extraordinary level of concentration. The immense importance attached to the Arhatthapala
Samadhi comes to light in the passages we have quoted. These discourses are abundant proof
of the fact that the Buddha has extolled this Samadhi in various ways. The verse beginning
with Nasanya Sanyi and Visanya Sanyi in particular points to this fact. On an early occasion we
gave only a clue to its meaning in the form of an allusion to our simile of the cinema.
That is to say, while one is watching a film show, if the cinema hall is fully illuminated
all of a sudden, one undergoes such an internal transformation that it becomes questionable
whether he is still seeing the film show. This is because his perception of the film show
has undergone a peculiar change. He is no longer conscious of a film show nor has he put an end
of consciousness. It is a strange paradox. His gaze is actually a vacant gaze. The verse in
question expresses such a vacant gaze. When the sixth sense basis of the Arhatthapala sees,
and the lustre of wisdom comes up, giving the conviction that all assets in the world are
empty, the vision in the Arhatthapala Samadhi is as vacant as that gaze of the man at the cinema.
It is neither conscious nor unconscious, non-unconscious nor totally devoid of consciousness. At that
level of concentration even this material form is abandoned. The line in the plan of joy in the
vāya-sutta, which we came across the other day, atarūpa, arūpācha, sukha-dukha, pamuchyati, and then from
form and formless and from pleasure and pain is you freed, can be better appreciated in the light of
the foreground discussion. With the relinquishment of all assets, even this body and the experience of a
form and of a formless as well as pleasure and pain cease altogether due to the cessation of contact.
That is why Nibbāna is called a bliss devoid of feeling, avidaita sukha. Now as to this vacant
gaze, there is much to be said, though one might think that it is not at all worth discussing about.
If someone asks us, what is the object of the gaze of one with such a vacant gaze,
what shall we say? The vacant gaze is, in fact, not established anywhere, apatita.
It has no existence, appavattā, and it is objectless, anāramana.
Even at the mention of these three terms, apatita, appavattā and anāramana,
some might recall those highly controversial discourses on Nibbāna.
Why do we call the vision of the arānta of vacant gaze? At the highest point of the development of the
three characteristics, impermanence, suffering and not-self, that is, through the three deliverances,
animitta, appanihitta and sunyata, the signless, the undirected and the void,
the arānta is now looking at the object with a penetrative gaze. That is why it is not possible
to say what he is looking at. It is a gaze that sees the cessation of the object, a gaze that
penetrates the object, as it were. When the cinema hall is fully illuminated, the mind of the one with
that vacant gaze at the film show does not accumulate the stuff that makes up a film.
Why? Because although cinema preparations are now stilled, cinema assets are relinquished,
and the craving and the passion for the cinema film have gone down, at least temporarily,
with the result that the cinema film has ceased for him and he is extinguished within.
That is why he is looking on with a vacant gaze. With this illustration, one can form an idea
about the inner transformation that occurs in the arānta. From the very outset, the meditator is
concerned with saṅkhāras or preparations. Hence, the term sabhasaṅkhāra samatha,
the stilling of our preparations, comes first. Instead of the arising aspect of preparations,
he attends to the cessation aspect, the furthest limit of which is nibbara. It is for that reason
that the term nirodha is directly applied to nibbara. Simply because we have recapitulated the terms
forming the theme of our sermons, some might think that the formula as such is some form of a gross object
of the mind. This, in fact, is the root of the misconception prevalent today. It is true that
the Buddha declared that the arānta has as his perception, attention and concentration the formula
beginning with etang-santang, etang-panitang etc. But this does not mean that the arāntini samadhi goes on
reciting the formula as we do at the beginning of every sermon. What it means is that the arānta reverts to
or reattains the realization he has already won through the lustre of wisdom, namely the realization
of the stealing of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets, the total abandonment of the five
aggregates, the destruction of craving, dispression, cessation and extinguishment. That is what one has
to understand by the saying that the arānta tends to nibbara as his object. The object is cessation,
Nirodha. Here is something that Mara cannot grasp that leaves him utterly clueless. This is why
Venerable Nandiya in the Nandiya Theragatha challenges Mara in the following verse.
The monk whose mind is always bright and gone to the fruit of arānthood, should you dare to
challenge that monk, O blacki, you only come to grief. Kanna blacki is one of the epithets of Mara.
Even gods and brahmas are unable to find out the object of the arānta's mind when he is in the
phalasamāpa, the attainment to the fruit. Mara can never discover it. That is why this attainment
is said to leave Mara clueless or deluded. Marasetam pamohana. All this is due to the uniqueness of
this level of concentration. The three deliverances Animitta, Appanitha and Sunyata are indeed
extraordinary and the verse Nasanya-sanyi refers to this arāta-pala-samādhi which is signless,
undirected and white. Usually one's vision alights somewhere or picks up some object or other.
But here is a range of vision that has no horizon. In general, there is a horizon at the furthest end
of our range of vision. Standing by the seaside or in a plane, one gazes upon the horizon where the
earth and sky meet. The whirling's range of vision in general has such a horizon. But the arānt's range
of vision as here described has no such horizon. That is why it is called anānta, endless or infinite.
The non-manifestative consciousness, endless, lustrous on all sides.
That vacant gaze is an endless perception. One who has it cannot be called conscious,
sanyi. Nor can he be called unconscious, visanyi in the worldly sense of the term. Nor is he
devoid of consciousness, asanyi. Nor has he put an end to consciousness, the bhūta-sanyi.
Let us now take up two verses which shed a flood of light on the fogha in discussion
and help illuminate the meaning of canonical passages that might come up later.
The two verses are from the arānta vagh of the dhammapada.
1. Those who have
know accumulations and understood fully the subject of food and whose feeding ground is
the void and the signless, they attract his heart to trace like that of birds in the sky.
He whose influxes are extinct and is unattached to nutriment, whose range is the deliverance
of the void and the signless, his path is hard to trace like that of birds in the sky.
The accumulation here mint is not of material things such as food.
It is the accumulation of karma and upadhi, assets.
The comprehension of food could be taken to imply the comprehension of all four nutrients,
namely cross-material food, contact, will and consciousness.
The feeding ground of such arahats is the void and the signless.
Hence their track is hard to trace like that of birds in the sky.
The term gati, which we rendered by track, has been differently interpreted in the commentary.
For the commentary, gati is the place where the arahant goes after death, his next born, so to speak.
But taken in conjunction with the simile used, gati obviously means the path, padam, taken by the birds in the sky.
It is the path they take that cannot be traced, not their destination.
Where the birds have gone could perhaps be traced with some difficulty.
They may have gone to their nests.
It is the path they went by that is deferred to as gati in this context.
Just as when birds fly through the sky, they do not leave behind any trace of a path.
Even so, in this concentration of the arahant, there is no object or sign of any continuity.
The second verse gives almost the same idea.
It is in singular and speaks of an arahant whose influxes are extinct and who is unattached to nutriment.
Here, in the simile about the birds in the sky, we find the word padam, path, used instead of gati, which makes it clear enough that it is not the destiny of the arahant that is spoken of.
The commentary, however, interprets both gati and padam as a reference to the arahant's destiny.
There is a tacit assumption of some mysterious Anupadi says Nibbana Dhatu.
But what we have here is a metaphor of considerable depth.
The reference is to that unique Samadhi.
The birds fly through the air symbolizes the flight of the mind.
In the case of others, the path taken by the mind can be traced through the object it takes, but not in this case.
The key word that highlights the metaphorical meaning of these verses is Gocharo.
Gocharo means pasture.
Now, in the case of cattle roaming in their pasture, one can trace them by their footsteps, by the path trodden.
What about the pasture of the arahants?
Of course, they too consume food to maintain their bodies, but their true pasture is the Arathya Phala Samadhi.
As soon as they get an opportunity, they take to this pasture.
Once they are well within this pasture, neither goats nor brahmas nor mar can find them.
That is why the path taken by the arahants in the Phala Samadhi cannot be traced like the track of birds in the sky.
Now, we have yet to discuss the subject of Saupadhi Sesa and Anupadhi Sesa in Manadha.
But even at this point, some clarity of understanding might emerge.
When the arahant passes away at the last moment of his life span, he brings his mind to this Arathya Phala Samadhi.
Then not even mark and trace him.
There is no possibility of a rebirth and that is the end of all.
It is this extinction that is referred to here.
This extinction is not something one gets in a world beyond.
It is a realization here and now in this world.
And the arahant, by way of blissful dwelling here and now, enjoys in his everyday life the supreme bliss of Nibbana that he had won through the incomparable deliverances of the mind.
